question: The Eighth Replenishment of the Global Fund to Fight AIDS, tuberculosis and malaria, which will finance the 2026–2028 cycle, will be announced at the G20 in South Africa. As HIV stands on the brink of a new surge, US cuts to the US President’s Emergency Plan for AIDS Relief and The United States Agency for International Development have already caused thousands of deaths.

In 2022, the Commission ranked seventh among donors, raising its contribution to EUR 715 million. For 2025, the target is to mobilise a total of USD 18 billion. If we fail, a reduction of just USD 3 billion would result in 3.75 million deaths and 66 million additional infections from one of these diseases. Europe would not be spared from these diseases.

The Commission’s EUR 715 million commitment for 2023–2025 was financed through the Neighbourhood, Development and International Cooperation Instrument, which is now threatened by budget cuts. Can Commission guarantee that it will raise its contribution to at least EUR 800 million, in order to offset disengagements, including within Europe, and to maintain global ambitions to combat these pandemics?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (4.3.2026) The EU has been a key supporter of the Global Fund since its establishment in 2001, with a total contribution of EUR 3.5 billion. The EU alone is currently its seventh public donor. Jointly with its Member States, the EU represents roughly a third of the total funding of the Global Fund.

EU commitment to Global Health and multilateralism is enshrined in EU Global Health Strategy adopted in November 20221 and in the EU Global Gateway Strategy2. It was captured in the declaration of the EU-AU Summit that took place in Luanda on 23-24 November 2025 and reaffirmed with the announcement of a new Global Health Resilience Initiative during the State of the Union in September 20253.

Global health challenges benefit from global responses. International support is also fundamental to complement the very much needed increase in domestic efforts in EU’s partner countries. Country ownership together with an integrated health system approach is the key to success.

This is why the Commission encourages the Global Fund and all relevant Global Health Initiatives to enhance their joint work and cooperation to accompany countries in their transition towards self-reliance, in line with the Lusaka Agenda.

The Commission could not financially commit during the Eight replenishment summit in November 2025 while expressing its strong support to the principles and to the mission of the Global Fund. The Commission has clearly shown willingness to continue being a major partner and intends to contribute to the new cycle of the Global Fund along the lines of previous cycles.
